headerBody: Mexico: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Mexican consumer-protection and police records — PROFECO (profeco.gob.mx), the Guardia Nacional, and state Fiscalía denuncias — plus r/MexicoTravel reports and verified local news. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Spanish phrases that shut them down.
quadHead: Four ways Mexico catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Arrival Taxi-Mafia Trap
quad.tl: A MXN 350 airport Uber becomes a USD 150 'private transfer' — or a MXN 2,500 'VIP taxi' when the real fare is MXN 900.

quad.title: The Fake-Visitax Shake-Down
quad.tl: The real Visitax is MXN 271 paid online before you fly — fake 'tax agents' at CUN demand USD 60 cash at the gate.

quad.title: The 'Private Yacht' to El Arco
quad.tl: A USD 30 group water-taxi to El Arco is pitched as a 'private yacht' at USD 400 a head; the official kiosk is three steps away.

quad.title: The Highway 307 Checkpoint
quad.tl: An invented 'infraction' at a Highway 307 rental-car stop: MXN 2,000–MXN 10,000 cash demanded 'to avoid problems.'

body: Mexico: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Mexican consumer-protection and police records — PROFECO (profeco.gob.mx), the Guardia Nacional, and state Fiscalía denuncias — plus r/MexicoTravel reports and verified local news. Not a recycled blog list.

114 specific scams across Mexico City, Cancún, Tulum, Cabo San Lucas, Puerto Vallarta and 14 more cities. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Spanish phrases that shut them down — written phonetically and in Spanish so you can show them on your phone.

Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — when a new edition ships, it appears in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Mexico relaxed, not braced.
